title: Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet I: Gilgamesh and the creation of Enkidu
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.4, Poem of Gilgamesh (ed. A. R. George, rev. G. Rozzi and E. Jiménez), SB I) + English of the eBL edition (A. R. George (eBL edition))
description: Standard Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet I: 231 of 300 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (6 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and A. R. George's English translation.
introduction:
The prologue praises Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, and the walls of his city. Because he oppresses his people, the gods create Enkidu, a wild man who lives with the animals. A trapper sends the prostitute Shamhat to him; she civilizes him and tells him of Gilgamesh, who meanwhile dreams of his coming.

The Standard Babylonian version of the epic, traditionally ascribed to the scholar Sin-leqi-unninni, was written on twelve tablets. Most surviving copies come from the libraries of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh (7th century BCE) and from Babylon and other Babylonian cities (7th-2nd century BCE). This page gives Tablet I in the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition by A. R. George (2022 and later revisions).

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/4/SB/I) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed copy of the work with the most signs preserved there. Commentaries and texts that only quote a line are never chosen. School and excerpt tablets are used only for lines that no photographed library copy preserves as well, and only where they carry the line as text; their sections say so. The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives; the notes give a key to every sign used on this page, and eBL's layout codes are written out in words (for example '(line break)' or '(blank space)'). Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is A. R. George's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the poem; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source. Where the tablet is broken, the English still translates the whole line of eBL's composite text; each section's note names the lines that are broken on its tablet.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 231 of the 300 lines of the eBL edition (77%), from 6 tablets in the British Museum: Rm.785, K.2756.C (Nineveh), K.4465 (Nineveh), K.8584 (Nineveh), K.2756.D (Nineveh), BM.38538.

Lines not shown. 69 of the 300 lines of the eBL edition are not shown, because no photographed copy of the work used here carries them: 19-47 (no photograph in eBL: IM.67577 (Iraq Museum); photograph does not show these lines (visual check): BM.34916); 48-51 (no photograph in eBL: IM.67577 (Iraq Museum); photograph does not show these lines (visual check): K.913, BM.34916); 52 (no photograph in eBL: IM.67577 (Iraq Museum); photograph does not show these lines (visual check): BM.34916); 82 (no photograph in eBL: VAT.17234 (Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin); photograph does not show these lines (visual check): BM.34916); 86 (no photograph in eBL: VAT.17234 (Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin); photograph does not show these lines (visual check): BM.34916); 145-154 (no photograph in eBL: K.2756.A); 208a-208b (not in the eBL Fragmentarium (no photograph there): IM.76973); 247-248 (photograph does not show these lines (visual check): K.913); 265-271 (photograph does not show these lines (visual check): K.913, BM.34916); 272 (photograph does not show these lines (visual check): BM.34916); 273-279 (photograph does not show these lines (visual check): K.913, BM.34916); 280 (photograph does not show these lines (visual check): BM.34916); 281-283 (photograph does not show these lines (visual check): K.913, BM.34916). A line is shown only on a photographed tablet that carries it as text. Commentaries and other texts that quote a line (letters, rituals, god lists) are not used as witnesses, because they carry it with explanations or inside another text; tablets without a photograph in eBL are not used, because the line could not be shown on its tablet.
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: A. R. George's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition (based on A. R. George, The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic, Oxford 2003). Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

Signs in the Akkadian: [ ] broken away; x illegible sign; # damaged sign; ? uncertain reading; ! sign corrected by the editor; ... broken signs of unknown number; ( ) signs perhaps broken away; { } determinative; < > sign omitted by the scribe, supplied by the editor; << >> sign written in error by the scribe; : divider sign written on the tablet.

98she fashioned Anu’s idea in her heart.
99Aruru washed her hands,
100she took a pinch of clay, she threw it down in the wild.
101In the wild she created Enkidu, the hero,

103All his body is matted with hair,
104he is adorned with tresses like a woman:
105the locks of his hair grow as thickly as Nissaba’s,

translation.text:
120The hunter opened [his mouth] to speak, saying [to his father:]
121‘My father, [there is a] certain fellow who has come [to us,]
122Mightiest in the [land, he possesses] strength,
123[his strength] is as mighty [as a lump of rock] from the sky.
124[He wanders always] over the hills,
125[always] with the herd [do I see him.]
126[Always] his feet [are found] by the water-hole,
127[I am afraid and so] I do not go up to him.
128[He has filled in the] pits that I dug,
129[he has uprooted] my snares that I laid.
130[He has set free from my grasp] the herd, the animals of the wild,
131[he will not let] me do the work of the wild.’
132[His father opened his mouth to speak], saying to the hunter:
133[Go, my son, to] Gilgamesh, [the offshoot sprung from] Uruk’s [midst!]
134[Make your way] into his presence,
135his strength [is as mig]hty [as a lump of rock from the sky.]
136[Take the road, set] your face [toward Uruk,]
137[…] the strength of a man!
138[Go, my son], bring [with you Šamhat the harlot,]
139[her allure is a match] for even the mighty!
140[When the herd comes] down [to] the water-hole,

translation.text:
171The animals arrived, they enjoyed the water,
172and also Enkidu himself, whose birth-place was the hills.
173Feeding on grass with the very gazelles,
174jostling at the water-hole with the herd,
175he enjoyed the water with the animals.
176(Then) Šamḫat saw him, the man-savage,
177a murderous fellow from the midst of the wild.
178‘This is he, Šamḫat! Uncradle your bosom;
179bare your sex so he may take in your charms!
180Do not show fear, take in his scent!
181He will see you and he will come up to you.
182Spread your clothing so he may lie on you,
183treat the man to the work of a woman!
184his herd will be estranged from him, though he grew up in its presence.
185His ‘love’ will caress and embrace you,
186Šamḫat let loose her skirts,
187she bared her sex and he took in her charms.
188She showed no fear, she took in his scent:
189she spread her clothing and he lay upon her.
190She treated the man to the work of a woman,
191his ‘love’ caressed and embraced her.
192For six days and seven nights Enkidu, erect, did couple with Šamḫat.
193After he was sated with her delights,
194he turned his face toward his herd.

translation.text:
195The gazelles saw Enkidu and they started running,
196the animals of the wild moved away from his person.
197Enkidu had defiled his body so pure,
198his legs stood still, though his herd was on the move.
199Enkidu was diminished, his running was not as before,
200but he had reason, he [was] wide of understanding.
201He came back and sat down at the feet of the harlot,
202watching the harlot, (observing) her features.
203Then his ears heard what the [harlot] was speaking,
204[as the harlot] said to him, to Enkidu:
205‘You are handsome, Enkidu, you are just like a god,
206why with the animals do you range through the wild?
207Come, I will lead you to Uruk-the-Sheepfold,
208to the sacred temple, the dwelling of Anu and Ištar!
209where Gilgameš is perfect in strength,
210and lords it over the menfolk like a wild bull!
211She talked to him and what she said found favour,
212his heart (now) wise was seeking a friend.
213Enkidu said to her, to the harlot:
214‘Come, Šamḫat, take me along
215to the sacred temple, the holy dwelling of Anu and Ištar,
216where Gilgameš is perfect in strength,
217and lords it over the menfolk like a wild bull!
218I will challenge him, for [my strength] is mighty,

219[I will vaunt] myself in Uruk, (saying) “I am the mightiest!”
220[there] I shall change the way things are ordered,
221[the one] born in the wild is mighty, he has strength.’
222‘Let [the people] see your face,
223[…that] exists I know indeed.
224Go, Enkidu, to Uruk-the-Sheepfold,
225where the young men are girt with waistbands.
226Every day [in Uruk] a festival is held,
227where the drums are repeatedly beaten,
228and the harlots are comely of figure,
229graced with charm, full of joy.
230Even the aged they rouse from their beds!
231O Enkidu, [who do not (yet)] know life –
232I will show you Gilgameš, the man so merry,
233look at him, regard his face!
234He is fair in manhood, he has dignified bearing,
235his whole person is graced with charm.
236He has a strength more mighty than you,
237he is unsleeping by day and by night.
238O Enkidu, get rid of your sinful intention,
239as for Gilgameš Šamaš loves him.

240Anu, Enlil and Ea broadened his wisdom:
241even before you came from the uplands,
242Gilgameš in Uruk was having dreams about you: –
243Gilgameš arose to reveal a dream, saying to his mother:
244“O mother, the dream that I saw in the course of this night –
245the stars of the heavens appeared before me,
246like a lump of rock from the sky one fell towards me.
249The land of Uruk was standing around [it],
250[the land was gathered] about it.
251A crowd [was jostling] before [it],
252[the menfolk were] thronging around it.
253They were kissing its feet [like a little] baby’s;
254[I loved it] like a wife and I caressed and embraced it.
255[I picked it up and] set it down at [your] feet,
256[and you, you] made it my equal.”
257[The mother of Gilgameš] was clever, she was wise, she knew everything, she said to her son;
258[Wild-Cow] Ninsun was clever, she was wise, she knew everything, she said to Gilgameš:
259“The stars of heaven [appeared] before you,
260[like a] lump of rock from the sky one fell toward you.
261You picked it up but it was too much for you,

On this tablet of lines 263-264 only one to three signs survive and line 262 is partly broken (square brackets and x in the Akkadian). The English of these lines translates eBL's composite text, so it includes words that are not preserved on this tablet but are restored from other manuscripts or by the editors. Square brackets in the English mark eBL's restorations in its composite text; words that survive on other tablets carry no brackets even where this tablet is broken.

translation.text:
284The mother of Gilgameš was clever, she was wise, she knew everything, she said to her son;
285Wild-Cow Ninsun was clever, she was wise, she knew everything, she said to Gilgameš:
286“My son, the axe you saw is a man,
287you will love him like a wife, and will caress and embrace him,
288and I, I shall make him your equal.
289A mighty companion will come to you, the saviour of (his) friend:
290he is the mightiest in the land, he has strength,
291his strength is as mighty as a lump of rock from the sky.”
292Gilgameš said to her, to his mother,
293“O mother, by Counsellor Enlil’s command may it befall me!
294I will acquire a friend, a counsellor,
295a friend, a counsellor, [I will] acquire!”
296[(Thus) he has] seen his dreams.’
297[After] Šamḫat told Enkidu the dreams of Gilgameš,
298the two of [them were making] love together.
